claim_text: Nicaea (325) was about the Arian controversy and the Nicene Creed — NOT the canon.

secondary_sources.citation: Henry Chadwick, The Early Church (Penguin, rev. ed. 1993)

counterargument: Popular skeptic accounts claim Constantine assembled the council to select or suppress scriptures. No primary source supports this; the council's agenda was exclusively Christological and disciplinary.
notes: This is the single most commonly encountered popular misconception in this corpus's subject area. Flagged in Method §2 reference table as explicitly false.

claim_text: The Merneptah Stele (c. 1208 BCE) is the first extrabiblical mention of Israel, as a people not a place.

secondary_sources.citation: James K. Hoffmeier, Israel in Egypt (Oxford University Press, 1997)
Frank J. Yurco, '3,200-Year-Old Picture of Israelites Found in Egypt,' Biblical Archaeology Review 16(5) 1990

notes: The determinative sign on 'Israel' in the stele marks it as a people/ethnic group rather than a territory, which is the basis for the 'people not a place' distinction. This is the scholarly consensus reading.

claim_text: Sennacherib's siege of Jerusalem (701 BCE) is the best-corroborated event in the Hebrew Bible.

secondary_sources.citation: William Hallo and K. Lawson Younger, eds., The Context of Scripture, vol. 2 (Brill, 2000)

counterargument: 'Best-corroborated' is a comparative claim. The Assyrian and biblical accounts diverge on outcome — Sennacherib claims tribute and withdrawal; the Bible records an angel destroying the army. The event's occurrence is corroborated; its outcome is contested between sources.
notes: Qualification added: corroboration is for the event, not the outcome. The 'best-corroborated' framing is defensible but should include this distinction in the public text.

claim_text: Paul's undisputed letters (c. 50–60 CE) are the earliest Christian writings that survive and contain no birth narrative, no empty tomb, no biography.

primary_sources.source: 1 Thessalonians, Galatians, 1–2 Corinthians, Romans, Philippians, Philemon
primary_sources.locator: Full texts; see also 1 Corinthians 15:3–8 for the resurrection tradition

secondary_sources.citation: Bart D. Ehrman, Forged (HarperOne, 2011)
Raymond E. Brown, An Introduction to the New Testament (Doubleday, 1997)

notes: The absence of birth narrative and empty tomb in Paul is a factual observation about Paul's surviving letters, not a theological claim. 1 Cor 15:3–8 does reference resurrection appearances, which should not be conflated with the empty-tomb narratives of the Gospels.

secondary_sources.citation: Paul L. Vasey and Nancy H. Bartlett, What can the Samoan Fa'afafine teach us about the Western concept of gender identity disorder in childhood? Perspectives in Biology and Medicine 50.4 (2007): 481–490
Paul L. Vasey et al., Traits of separation anxiety in childhood: a retrospective study of Samoan men, women, and fa'afafine, Archives of Sexual Behavior 40 (2011): 511–517

counterargument: The cited studies use Western analytical labels such as transgender or alternative gender role; the module does not assume those are exact translations of the Samoan category.
notes: Terminology qualification is part of the public claim context.

claim_text: Muhammad Azfar Nisar documents a heterogeneous gender-nonconforming community and significant internal distinctions among umbrella terms.

secondary_sources.citation: Muhammad Azfar Nisar, Governing Thirdness: State, Society, and Non-binary Identities (Cambridge University Press, 2021/2022)
secondary_sources.locator: Book description and chapter 2 summary; DOI 10.1017/9781009030045

counterargument: Khawaja sira, hijra, and related terms have context-dependent meanings; the module does not treat all South Asian gender-nonconforming people as one uniform identity.

claim_text: “Two-Spirit” is treated as a modern umbrella adopted in 1990, not back-projected as the historical name of every Indigenous tradition.

secondary_sources.citation: Gregory D. Smithers, Reclaiming Two-Spirits: Sexuality, Spiritual Renewal & Sovereignty in Native America (Beacon Press, 2022)
secondary_sources.locator: Smithsonian catalog summary: umbrella term began being used in 1990 and discusses tribally specific identities; https://www.si.edu/es/object/reclaiming-two-spirits-sexuality-spiritual-renewal-sovereignty-native-america-gregory-d-smithers%3Asiris_sil_1173748

secondary_sources.citation: Sue-Ellen Jacobs, Wesley Thomas, and Sabine Lang, eds., Two-Spirit People: Native American Gender Identity, Sexuality, and Spirituality (University of Illinois Press, 1997)
secondary_sources.locator: Smithsonian catalog contents and summary; nation-specific cases and critique of Western categories

counterargument: Two-Spirit is useful as a contemporary umbrella, but it cannot substitute for specific Indigenous nations' historical categories, meanings, or terminology.

claim_text: Kathryn M. Ringrose argues that Byzantine eunuchs occupied a distinct gender configuration beyond a simple male/female social binary, especially in courtly contexts.

secondary_sources.citation: Kathryn M. Ringrose, The Perfect Servant: Eunuchs and the Social Construction of Gender in Byzantium (University of Chicago Press, 2003; Oxford Academic online ed. 2004)

counterargument: This is Ringrose's modern analytical interpretation of Byzantine evidence, not a claim that Byzantine sources used contemporary Western gender terminology.

claim_text: The National Academies describes sex as multidimensional: multiple anatomical and physiological traits usually align but do not always do so.

secondary_sources.citation: National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, Measuring Sex, Gender Identity, and Sexual Orientation (National Academies Press, 2022)
secondary_sources.locator: Summary table defining sex as a multidimensional construct; https://nap.nationalacademies.org/catalog/26424/measuring-sex-gender-identity-and-sexual-orientation

secondary_sources.citation: David Andrew Griffiths, Diagnosing sex: Intersex surgery and sex change in Britain 1930–1955, Sexualities 21.3 (2018): 476–495
Luke Muschialli et al., Perspectives on conducting sex-normalising intersex surgeries conducted in infancy: A systematic review, PLOS Global Public Health 4.8 (2024): e0003568
secondary_sources.locator: Systematic review of elective childhood interventions; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39197054/

notes: The public module explicitly states that intersex is not itself a third-gender category and keeps sex traits separate from social gender.

claim_text: Svärd and Nissinen find enough evidence for unconventional gender performance and gender-boundary transgression associated with the assinnu in Ištar's cult.

secondary_sources.citation: Saana Svärd and Martti Nissinen, '(Re)constructing the Image of the Assinnu,' in Studying Gender in the Ancient Near East, ed. Saana Svärd and Agnès Garcia-Ventura (Eisenbrauns/Penn State University Press, 2018), 373–411
Ilan Peled, 'Visualizing Masculinities: The Gala, Hegemony, and Mesopotamian Iconography,' Near Eastern Archaeology 79.3 (2016): 158–165
secondary_sources.locator: Abstract and discussion of non-hegemonic masculinity; DOI 10.5615/neareastarch.79.3.0158

counterargument: The evidence does not establish that assinnu uniformly map onto a modern transgender identity, nor does it decisively establish castration or a specific same-sex sexual role. The public text therefore limits the claim to unconventional gender performance and boundary transgression.

claim_text: Hatshepsut was a woman who ruled as pharaoh.

primary_sources.source: Metropolitan Museum of Art, Hatshepsut in a Devotional Attitude, object 29.3.1
Metropolitan Museum of Art, The Female Pharaoh Hatshepsut, object 29.3.2

notes: The same Met records document masculine kingly representation alongside feminine grammatical forms and Hatshepsut's female personal name. The module explicitly does not infer a third-gender category.

claim_text: Deuteronomy 23:1 excludes a man whose genitalia have been crushed or cut from the assembly of YHWH.
notes: The paired public case contrasts Deuteronomy's exclusion with Isaiah 56:3–5's promise to covenant-keeping eunuchs. No historical dating or causal claim is inferred from the textual contrast.

claim_text: Rabbinic legal texts explicitly discuss persons who are not definitely classifiable as male or female in particular legal contexts.

primary_sources.locator: Tumtum and androgynos are distinguished from definite male and definite female for valuation law

secondary_sources.citation: Jane L. Kanarek, 'Rewriting ‘Arakhin: Women and Tannaitic Vows of Valuation,' AJS Review 40.2 (2016): 261–277
Marianne Schleicher, 'Constructions of Sex and Gender: Attending to Androgynes and Tumtumim Through Jewish Scriptural Use,' Literature and Theology 25.4 (2011): 422–435

counterargument: Modern summaries that call these 'six genders' risk importing contemporary identity categories into body- and law-based rabbinic classifications. Scholarship also emphasizes that the male/female binary remains structurally important in halakhic reasoning.

claim_text: The galli are documented as self-castrated priests associated with feminine-coded dress and appearance, and Roman authors often portrayed them as violating normative masculinity.

secondary_sources.citation: Chris Mowat, 'Don't be a Drag, Just be a Priest: The Clothing and Identity of the Galli of Cybele in the Roman Republic and Empire,' Gender & History 33.2 (2021): 296–313
Marika Rauhala, 'Obscena Galli Praesentia: Dehumanizing Cybele's Eunuch-Priests through Disgust,' in The Ancient Emotion of Disgust (Oxford University Press, 2016), 235–252

counterargument: The surviving literary record is frequently hostile, and describing the galli as nonbinary is a modern analytical interpretation rather than an attested ancient self-identification.

claim_text: Canon 1 distinguishes involuntary or medically necessary castration from voluntary self-castration.

primary_sources.source: First Council of Nicaea (325 CE), Canon 1
primary_sources.locator: Canon 1; English translation in Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Series II, vol. 14; https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/3801.htm

notes: The rule concerns castration and clerical eligibility. The module explicitly does not infer gender identity from it.

claim_text: Philo of Alexandria repeatedly uses eunuchism and castration in exegetical and philosophical discussions of male and female categories.

secondary_sources.citation: Ra‘anan Abusch, 'Eunuchs and Gender Transformation: Philo’s Exegesis of the Joseph Narrative,' in Eunuchs in Antiquity and Beyond (2002), 103–122

counterargument: This material shows Philo's exegetical and philosophical use of eunuchism; it does not by itself establish a third social gender among Alexandrian Jews.

claim_text: Acts 8 repeatedly identifies an Ethiopian royal official as a eunuch and depicts his baptism without narrating a change in that designation.

secondary_sources.citation: Brittany E. Wilson, 'Neither Male nor Female: The Ethiopian Eunuch in Acts 8.26–40,' New Testament Studies 60.3 (2014): 403–422

counterargument: Wilson's description of the figure as boundary-crossing is a contextual literary interpretation; it is not a recovered first-person gender identity.

claim_text: Matthew 19:12 distinguishes eunuchs born so, eunuchs made so by others, and those who made themselves eunuchs for the kingdom; Eusebius later reports that Origen interpreted the verse literally enough to castrate himself.

secondary_sources.citation: Ronald E. Heine, 'Origen and his Opponents on Matthew 19:12,' Studia Patristica 56 (2013): 123–128

counterargument: Modern scholars dispute the historical reliability of the Origen self-castration story. The registry treats Matthew as direct evidence and Origen as disputed reception history.

claim_text: Rabbinic texts classify aylonit and forms of saris through bodily signs, fertility, and legal consequences.

secondary_sources.citation: Sarra Lev, 'How the Aylonit Got Her Sex,' AJS Review 31.2 (2007): 297–316

counterargument: Lev argues that the constructed signs can cross sex/gender markers, while also observing that rabbinic law does not generally treat the aylonit as a distinct gender identity. Modern intersex/trans labels are not direct equivalents.

claim_text: The Kāmasūtra explicitly describes persons of a 'third nature' and distinguishes two forms, including one characterized by feminine dress, speech, manner, and a specific sexual/economic role.

primary_sources.locator: 2.9.6–24; trans. Wendy Doniger and Sudhir Kakar, Oxford University Press, 2002

secondary_sources.citation: Wendy Doniger, 'The Third Nature: Gender Inversions in the Kamasutra,' in On Hinduism (Oxford University Press, 2014), 314–329

counterargument: Tṛtīyā prakṛti belongs to ancient Sanskrit erotic taxonomy. It should not be treated as automatically equivalent to contemporary transgender, nonbinary, or gay identity categories.

claim_text: Surviving naming, dress, office, and textual evidence generally categorized Mughal khwāja sarās as men, despite castration and distinctive bodily characteristics.

secondary_sources.citation: Emma Kalb, 'A eunuch at the threshold: mediating access and intimacy in the Mughal world,' Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society 33.3 (2023): 747–768

counterargument: The term 'eunuch' has historically collapsed different South Asian categories. Kalb distinguishes Mughal enslaved, castrated khwāja sarās from hijra communities and notes that Mughal evidence does not support treating the former as a third gender.

claim_text: Part II of the Criminal Tribes Act of 1871 created registers of persons the colonial state classified as 'eunuchs', penalized registered persons for appearing publicly in feminine dress or performing, and restricted guardianship/adoption.

secondary_sources.citation: Jessica Hinchy, Governing Gender and Sexuality in Colonial India: The Hijra, c.1850–1900 (Cambridge University Press, 2019)

notes: Public text distinguishes the colonial statutory category 'eunuch' from Hijra identity and notes variation in enforcement and resistance.

claim_text: British colonial administration used the English category 'eunuch' to group distinct South Asian populations and defined the legal category in male terms, including persons 'of the male sex' judged impotent.

secondary_sources.citation: Jessica Hinchy, Power, perversion and panic: eunuchs, colonialism and modernity in North India (ANU PhD thesis, 2013)
Jessica Hinchy, Governing Gender and Sexuality in Colonial India: The Hijra, c.1850–1900 (Cambridge University Press, 2019)

counterargument: The category was not internally coherent and did not translate one indigenous identity. The public text therefore treats it as colonial administrative reclassification rather than a neutral description.

claim_text: Spanish missionary and military sources described Indigenous people in Alta California who dressed and worked in feminine-coded roles, frequently under the colonial label joya, and missionaries explicitly expected missionization to eliminate those practices.

secondary_sources.citation: Deborah A. Miranda, 'Extermination of the Joyas: Gendercide in Spanish California,' GLQ 16.1–2 (2010): 253–284

Diana Roselly Pérez Gerardo, 'Hombres que vivían como las mujeres en la Alta California del siglo XVIII: Coyas/joyas, cuút o uluqi, ¿sodomitas, hermafroditas o amaricados?,' Historia Crítica 93 (2024): 3–24
Mario Alberto G. Magaña Mancillas and Raúl Balbuena Bello, 'Joyas o indios vestidos de mujer en la Alta California colonial: reflexiones sobre la identidad de género,' Cuicuilco 17.49 (2010): 243–259

counterargument: The Spanish label joya collapsed distinct nation-specific roles and terms. Miranda's term 'gendercide' is an attributed interpretation and is not applied automatically to every California Indigenous community.

claim_text: Federal Indian boarding schools imposed sex-segregated dress, labor, domestic training, and Victorian gender norms as part of forced assimilation.

secondary_sources.citation: K. Tsianina Lomawaima, 'Domesticity in the federal Indian schools: the power of authority over mind and body,' American Ethnologist 20.2 (1993): 227–240
David Wallace Adams, Education for Extinction: American Indians and the Boarding School Experience, 1875–1928

Teresa Evans-Campbell, Karina L. Walters, Cynthia R. Pearson, and Christopher D. Campbell, 'Indian Boarding School Experience, Substance Use, and Mental Health among Urban Two-Spirit American Indian/Alaska Natives,' American Journal of Drug and Alcohol Abuse 38.5 (2012): 421–427

counterargument: Effects varied by nation, school, period, family, and individual, and the historical record also documents resistance. The public text does not claim total or uniform erasure of Indigenous gender systems.

claim_text: Protestant missionaries promoted permanent sexually exclusive heterosexual marriage and a more patriarchal domestic model in Hawai‘i, contributing to changes in gender and sexual relations during the early nineteenth century.

secondary_sources.citation: Sally Engle Merry, 'Early Pacific Encounters and Masculinity: War, Sex, and Christianity in Hawai‘i,' Current Anthropology 62.S23 (2021)

counterargument: Merry treats the transformation as multicausal and negotiated, involving Hawaiian chiefs, commerce, demographic catastrophe, political change, and existing institutions as well as missionaries. The module does not yet make a māhū-specific suppression claim.

claim_text: British clinicians were performing surgical interventions on people with atypical sex characteristics before the Johns Hopkins protocols associated with John Money became internationally influential.

secondary_sources.citation: David Andrew Griffiths, 'Diagnosing sex: Intersex surgery and sex change in Britain 1930–1955,' Sexualities 21.3 (2018): 476–495
secondary_sources.locator: Full article, especially discussion of Broster and pre-1955 British practice; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5836525/

counterargument: This does not mean British practice was uniform or identical to the later Johns Hopkins model. Griffiths emphasizes changing combinations of surgical, endocrine, social, legal, and psychological reasoning.

claim_text: John Money, Joan G. Hampson, and John L. Hampson published formal recommendations in 1955 on sex assignment, change of sex, and psychological management for people then described as hermaphroditic.

primary_sources.source: John Money, Joan G. Hampson, and John L. Hampson, 'Hermaphroditism: recommendations concerning assignment of sex, change of sex and psychologic management,' Bulletin of the Johns Hopkins Hospital 97.4 (1955): 284–300

secondary_sources.citation: Sandra Eder, 'Gender and Cortisone: Clinical Practice and Transatlantic Exchange in the Medical Management of Intersex in the 1950s,' Bulletin of the History of Medicine 92.4 (2018): 604–633
David Andrew Griffiths, 'Diagnosing sex: Intersex surgery and sex change in Britain 1930–1955,' Sexualities 21.3 (2018): 476–495
secondary_sources.locator: Sections on Money/Hampson protocols and British precursors; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5836525/

counterargument: The Hopkins model was highly influential but not the sole origin of intersex medical management; historians document earlier and transatlantic clinical precedents.

claim_text: Intersex patient activism in the 1990s challenged secrecy, stigma, and unwanted genital surgery; the 2006 international medical consensus explicitly recognized patient-advocacy and ethical concerns and proposed 'disorders of sex development' as new clinical terminology.

secondary_sources.citation: Intersex Society of North America, 'What's the history behind the intersex rights movement?'
Peter A. Lee et al., 'Consensus Statement on Management of Intersex Disorders,' Pediatrics 118.2 (2006): e488–e500

counterargument: The 2006 consensus did not settle disputes over genital surgery, consent, nomenclature, or medicalization. The claim is an institutional-shift claim, not a claim of resolved consensus on all treatment questions.

claim_text: New York City rules for changing sex designations on birth certificates changed substantially between 1965 and 2006, with administrative reasoning shifting from fraud prevention toward evidence of permanence.

secondary_sources.citation: Paisley Currah and Lisa Jean Moore, 'We Won't Know Who You Are: Contesting Sex Designations in New York City Birth Certificates,' Hypatia 24.3 (2009): 113–135
secondary_sources.locator: Article abstract and historical analysis; DOI 10.1111/j.1527-2001.2009.01048.x

counterargument: This is a New York City case study, not a description of every U.S. state or every identity document.

claim_text: German civil-status law evolved from allowing a blank sex entry for some people, to a 2017 constitutional ruling requiring a positive option beyond male/female when sex registration is mandatory, to the 2018 'divers' entry and a 2024 self-determination law allowing changes among available gender-marker options or deletion of the marker.

primary_sources.source: German Federal Constitutional Court, Order of 10 October 2017, 1 BvR 2019/16
Act on Self-Determination With Regard to Gender Markers (SBGG), 19 June 2024

counterargument: The 2017 case concerned a person with atypical sex development, while the 2024 law created a broader identity-based declaration process; the later law should not be retroactively read into the earlier regime.

claim_text: Nepal has officially recognized a third-gender/'other' category in state documents since implementation of the 2007 Supreme Court decision, and current passport instructions provide M, F, and X options tied to the applicant's citizenship certificate.

primary_sources.source: Government of Nepal report to the United Nations
primary_sources.locator: Report states official recognition of third-gender category since 2007 and citizenship 'other' implementation; OHCHR document repository
Current passport instructions: M male, F female, X other; https://nepalpassport.gov.np/en/process/process-40

counterargument: The administrative labels 'other' and X do not establish one uniform social identity among all people using them.

claim_text: As of 28 September 2026, the U.S. State Department issues only M or F passport markers matching sex at birth and no X marker, while Australia and New Zealand continue to provide X marker options under their passport systems.

primary_sources.source: U.S. Department of State, 'Sex Markers in Passports'
Australian Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade, passport policy
primary_sources.locator: Sex (gender) on Australian travel document; current policy page accessed 2026-09-28; https://www.dfat.gov.au/about-us/publications/corporate/passports/passport-policy

primary_sources.source: New Zealand Passports, 'Change your gender in your passport'

counterargument: This is a dated administrative-policy comparison. U.S. policy is affected by executive action and litigation, while Australia and New Zealand apply distinct national definitions and procedures.

claim_text: Ifi Amadiume documents Nnobi institutions in which women could occupy socially masculine kinship and political positions described analytically as 'male daughters' and 'female husbands'.

secondary_sources.citation: Ifi Amadiume, Male Daughters, Female Husbands: Gender and Sex in an African Society (1987; new ed. 2015)
secondary_sources.locator: Book argument summarized in University of Chicago Press catalog description

secondary_sources.citation: Lorelle Semley, 'When We Discovered Gender: A Retrospective on Ifi Amadiume’s Male Daughters, Female Husbands,' Journal of West African History 3.2 (2017): 117–123

counterargument: Amadiume's wider claims about precolonial gender are influential and debated. These roles are treated as kinship/status positions, not automatic modern gender identities or a continent-wide African model.

claim_text: Regina Smith Oboler documents Nandi women who married wives, paid bridewealth, managed family property, and became the social/legal fathers of their wives' children in order to secure heirs.

secondary_sources.citation: Regina Smith Oboler, 'Is the Female Husband a Man? Woman/Woman Marriage among the Nandi of Kenya,' Ethnology 19.1 (1980): 69–88

counterargument: The institution is primarily about kinship, inheritance, property, and fatherhood and should not automatically be mapped onto modern lesbian or transgender identity.

claim_text: Rudolf Gaudio documents 'yan daudu as a recognized category of feminine men in Hausa Muslim society with distinctive social networks, speech practices, occupations, and relationships to women's spaces and bori traditions.

secondary_sources.citation: Rudolf Pell Gaudio, Allah Made Us: Sexual Outlaws in an Islamic African City (Wiley-Blackwell, 2009)
secondary_sources.locator: Ethnography of 'yan daudu in Hausa-speaking northern Nigeria

counterargument: The category intersects gender expression, sexuality, class, religion, and urban social life and is not treated as a direct equivalent of gay man, trans woman, or third gender.

claim_text: Douglas Oliver's reconstruction of late Indigenous Tahitian society reports institutionalized tolerance for anatomically male people who adopted female behavioral roles, identified as māhū.

secondary_sources.citation: Douglas L. Oliver, Ancient Tahitian Society (University of Hawai‘i Press, 1974), vol. 2, ch. 15
secondary_sources.locator: Open-access JSTOR edition, discussion of māhū in chapter 15

secondary_sources.citation: Makiko Kuwahara, 'Living as and Living with Māhū and Raerae: Geopolitics, Sex, and Gender in the Society Islands,' in Gender on the Edge (2014), 93–114

counterargument: Oliver's account is a historical reconstruction using early-contact sources; modern māhū and raerae categories are not assumed to be unchanged survivals from the eighteenth century.

claim_text: Ethnographic scholarship documents fakaleitī as a recognized Tongan category involving feminine presentation and social roles among people assigned male.

secondary_sources.citation: Mary K. Good, 'The Fokisi and the Fakaleitī: Provocative Performances in Tonga,' in Gender on the Edge (2014), 213–240
Niko Besnier, 'Transgenderism, Locality, and the Miss Galaxy Beauty Pageant in Tonga,' American Ethnologist 29.3 (2002): 534–566

counterargument: Fakaleitī identities are heterogeneous and culturally specific; the term is not treated as a one-to-one translation of 'trans woman'.

claim_text: Tom Boellstorff documents waria as a widely recognized Indonesian feminine-male/transfeminine social category embedded in Indonesian national culture.

secondary_sources.citation: Tom Boellstorff, 'Playing Back the Nation: Waria, Indonesian Transvestites,' Cultural Anthropology 19.2 (2004): 159–195

counterargument: Boellstorff explicitly cautions against treating waria as a universal third gender; his analysis describes the category as a form of male femininity within Indonesian national culture.
